question: The members of a private company wish to deal with three matters quickly by written resolution: adopting new articles, approving a loan to a director, and removing a director from office. The solicitor advises that one of the three cannot be done in that way. Which is it?
options: Adopting the new articles, because a constitutional change requires a general meeting.
Approving the loan, because the memorandum must be laid before a general meeting.
Removing the director, because removal must be dealt with at a general meeting.
None of them, because a private company may pass any resolution in writing.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Removing the director, because removal must be dealt with at a general meeting): removal of a director and removal of an auditor are the two matters excluded from the written resolution procedure, because the officer concerned has a right to make representations and be heard. Option A is wrong because new articles may be adopted by written special resolution without any meeting.

question: A private company wishes to hold a general meeting in six days' time to pass a special resolution. Its two members hold the voting shares as to ninety five per cent and five per cent, and both are willing to attend on that date. What must the company obtain?
options: Nothing, because fourteen days' notice is required only for an annual general meeting.
The written consent of the holder of five per cent of the voting shares.
An order of the court permitting the meeting to be held on shorter notice.
Consent to short notice from a majority in number holding ninety per cent of shares.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Consent to short notice from a majority in number holding ninety per cent of shares): the default notice period for a general meeting of a private company is fourteen clear days, and a meeting may be held on shorter notice only with the agreement of a majority in number of the members holding at least ninety per cent of the voting shares. Option B is wrong because consent must come from a majority in number as well as the required percentage of shares.

question: A minority shareholder holding six per cent of the voting capital of a private company wants a general meeting called to consider the removal of a director. The board refuses to call one, saying that only the directors may convene a general meeting. What is the correct position?
options: Members holding five per cent of the voting capital may require a meeting to be called.
Only the board may call a general meeting of a private company limited by shares.
The shareholder must first obtain permission from the court before convening a meeting.
The shareholder must hold ten per cent of the voting capital to require a meeting.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Members holding five per cent of the voting capital may require a meeting to be called): the Companies Act 2006 lets members with at least five per cent of the paid up voting capital require the directors to call a general meeting, and this matters because a director can be removed only at a meeting. Option B would leave the members with no route to remove a director whom the board supports.

question: A shareholder in a family company complains that she dislikes the board's cautious dividend policy. The policy follows the articles and applies in exactly the same way to every shareholder, including the majority. She wants to petition on the ground of unfair prejudice. What is the main difficulty?
options: A petition may only be brought by a member holding at least ten per cent.
She must show both unfairness and prejudice, judged against the members' bargain.
A petition may only be presented once the company has already entered liquidation.
The only remedy sought must be damages, which the court has no power to award.
explanation: The correct answer is B (She must show both unfairness and prejudice, judged against the members' bargain): a section 994 petition requires conduct that is both unfair and prejudicial to the petitioner's interests as a member, measured against the terms on which the members agreed to associate. A policy applied evenly and in accordance with the articles is unlikely to qualify. Option A is wrong because there is no minimum shareholding for a petition.

question: A petition under section 994 succeeds. The petitioner holds a minority stake in a small private company and no longer wishes to be involved in the business at all. The court is now considering what order it should make on the petition. What is the usual remedy?
options: An order winding the company up and distributing any surplus among the members.
An order that the company pay the petitioner damages for her lost dividends.
An order that the majority buy the petitioner's shares at a proper valuation.
An order removing the offending directors and appointing an independent board instead.
explanation: The correct answer is C (An order that the majority buy the petitioner's shares at a proper valuation): the court has a wide discretion, but the standard outcome is a share purchase order, which releases the minority from a company she can no longer work in. Option A is available in principle on a separate just and equitable winding up petition, but it destroys the business and is treated as a remedy of last resort.

question: A member of a company believes a director has diverted a contract to a business of his own, causing the company loss. She wants the wrong put right and asks whether she can sue in the company's name. Which statement correctly describes a derivative claim?
options: She sues in her own name and any damages recovered belong to her personally.
She may sue only if she already held her shares when the wrong was committed.
She may bring the claim without any permission, provided the company remains solvent.
She sues on the company's behalf with permission, and any remedy is the company's.
explanation: The correct answer is D (She sues on the company's behalf with permission, and any remedy is the company's): a derivative claim is brought by a member in respect of a wrong done to the company, the court's permission to continue is required, and any recovery belongs to the company rather than the claimant. Option A confuses a derivative claim with a personal claim, and is the distinction that decides which route a minority client should take.

question: A solicitor is choosing between a section 994 petition and a derivative claim for a minority client. The client wants a clean exit from the company with money in her own hand, rather than a recovery that stays inside the company. Which route fits her aim?
options: A section 994 petition, whose usual outcome is a purchase of her shares.
A derivative claim, because any sum recovered is paid directly to the claimant.
A derivative claim, because the court may order the majority to buy her out.
Either route, because both of them produce a payment made personally to the member.
explanation: The correct answer is A (A section 994 petition, whose usual outcome is a purchase of her shares): the petition is a personal remedy and the standard order is that the majority buy the petitioner out, giving her the exit she wants. Option B is wrong because the whole nature of a derivative claim is that the company, not the member, receives the remedy.

question: The directors of a private company that has only one class of ordinary shares wish to allot further shares of that same class. The articles say nothing at all about allotment. The company secretary asks whether a members' resolution is needed before the board may allot. What is the position?
options: An ordinary resolution granting authority is required before the directors may allot shares.
The directors may allot without further authority, the articles not restricting them.
A special resolution is required, because an allotment alters the company's share capital.
The directors may allot only after offering the shares to the company's secured creditors.
explanation: The correct answer is B (The directors may allot without further authority, the articles not restricting them): where a private company has only one class of shares, the directors may exercise the power to allot shares of that class unless the articles say otherwise. Option A states the position for a company with more than one class, or where the articles impose a restriction, which is not this company.

question: A private company proposes to allot new ordinary shares for cash to an outside investor. The existing shareholders have not been offered any of the new shares and no resolution has been passed about pre emption. One of them objects to the allotment. What is the correct analysis?
options: Pre emption rights apply only where shares are allotted for a non cash asset.
Pre emption rights bind the company only if they are written into its articles.
The shareholder's remedy is a petition alleging unfair prejudice rather than pre emption.
Equity securities allotted for cash must first be offered to the existing shareholders.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Equity securities allotted for cash must first be offered to the existing shareholders): the statutory right of pre emption requires equity securities allotted for cash to be offered to existing holders in proportion to their existing holdings unless the right is disapplied. Option B is wrong because the right arises under the Companies Act 2006 itself and applies whether or not the articles mention it.

question: A company wants to allot shares for cash to a new investor without offering them to the existing members first. The board asks how the statutory pre emption rights can properly be set aside for that particular allotment. Which answer is correct?
options: By an ordinary resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights.
By a board resolution recording that the allotment is in the company's best interests.
By a special resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights.
By the written consent of the investor to whom the new shares are to be allotted.
explanation: The correct answer is C (By a special resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights): disapplication requires the seventy five per cent threshold, because the members are giving up a protection the statute gives them. Option A applies the ordinary resolution threshold, which would let a bare majority strip the minority of the very right that protects it against dilution.

question: A shareholder signs a stock transfer form and hands it, with her share certificate, to a buyer who pays the agreed price. The buyer has not yet been entered in the register of members. The company then declares a dividend. Who is entitled to be paid that dividend by the company?
options: The seller, because legal title passes only on registration in the register of members.
The buyer, because he holds the signed stock transfer form and the share certificate.
The buyer, because legal and beneficial ownership both pass on delivery of the form.
Neither of them, because the dividend must be held back until the register is updated.
explanation: The correct answer is A (The seller, because legal title passes only on registration in the register of members): a transfer binds the company only once the buyer is registered, so until then the seller remains the member the company must pay, holding the benefit for the buyer. Option C is wrong because delivery of the executed form passes the beneficial interest but not the legal title the company recognises.

question: A company's relevant accounts show accumulated realised profits of two hundred thousand pounds and accumulated realised losses of one hundred and eighty thousand pounds. The board wishes to pay a dividend of fifty thousand pounds to its shareholders this month. What is the correct advice to the board?
options: The dividend is lawful, because realised profits comfortably exceed fifty thousand pounds.
The dividend is unlawful, because profits available for distribution are only twenty thousand.
The dividend is lawful, provided the members first approve it by special resolution.
The dividend is unlawful, because a dividend cannot exceed the current year's trading profit.
explanation: The correct answer is B (The dividend is unlawful, because profits available for distribution are only twenty thousand): profits available for distribution are accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses, so the fund here is twenty thousand pounds and a fifty thousand pound dividend exceeds it. Option A looks only at the profits side of the calculation and ignores the accumulated losses that must be deducted.

question: A company pays a dividend at a time when it has no distributable profits. One recipient is a non executive director who had seen the management accounts and knew the position. Another is a passive investor who received nothing beyond the payment advice. What is the position on repayment?
options: Both must repay, because an unlawful dividend is recoverable from every recipient.
Neither must repay, because the fault lies with the directors who authorised the payment.
The recipient who knew the position must repay; the passive investor need not.
Both may keep the dividend, but the directors must make good the company's loss.
explanation: The correct answer is C (The recipient who knew the position must repay; the passive investor need not): a member is liable to repay an unlawful distribution where he knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, that it was unlawful, so knowledge is the test. Option A ignores that requirement, and the directors who authorised the payment may separately be liable to make good the loss.

question: The board of a private company wishes to pay a dividend at the half year, without waiting for the annual accounts or for a members' meeting. The finance director asks whether the members must vote on the payment before it can be made. What is the correct advice?
options: An interim dividend may be paid by the board without any members' resolution.
Any dividend requires an ordinary resolution of the members before it may be paid.
An interim dividend requires a special resolution because the annual accounts are unavailable.
The board may pay an interim dividend only if the articles are first amended.
explanation: The correct answer is A (An interim dividend may be paid by the board without any members' resolution): a final dividend is declared by the members by ordinary resolution on the board's recommendation, but an interim dividend is decided on by the directors alone. The payment must still come out of profits available for distribution. Option B states the rule for final dividends and applies it too widely.

question: A private company wants to buy back the shares of a departing shareholder. It has substantial distributable profits and does not wish to raise any new money for the purpose. The board asks which funds may lawfully be used for the purchase. Which answer is correct?
options: Only the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose.
Any of the company's cash, because a buyback is an ordinary trading payment.
Only capital, and then only if the strict statutory procedure has been followed.
Its distributable profits, the ordinary source for a purchase of its own shares.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Its distributable profits, the ordinary source for a purchase of its own shares): a company may buy its own shares out of distributable profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue made for the purpose, and a private company may in addition use capital under a strict procedure. Option C treats the exceptional capital route as the only one available, when the company already has the profits to fund the purchase.

question: An investor asks whether he should subscribe for newly issued shares or instead buy shares from an existing member. He wants the route that puts fresh money into the company itself rather than into another shareholder's pocket. Which answer correctly explains the difference?
options: A transfer, because the consideration passes to the company on registration of the buyer.
An allotment, because the subscription money is paid to the company itself.
Both, because the company receives the price and then accounts to the seller for it.
Neither, because consideration for shares is held on trust for the members generally.
explanation: The correct answer is B (An allotment, because the subscription money is paid to the company itself): on an allotment the company creates and issues new shares and receives the subscription monies, whereas on a transfer an existing share simply changes hands and the price goes to the seller. Option A reverses the two, and the distinction decides whether the transaction raises capital or merely changes the ownership of the company.

question: A private company's articles give the directors a discretion to refuse to register a transfer of shares. A member transfers her shares to her brother and the directors decline to register him. The brother says the transfer is complete because the stock transfer form was properly executed. What is the position?
options: The transfer is complete, because execution and delivery pass the full title to him.
The transfer is complete, because directors may not refuse a transfer to a family member.
He is not a member, because the company is bound only on registration of the transfer.
He is a member, but has no right to vote until the register has been updated.
explanation: The correct answer is C (He is not a member, because the company is bound only on registration of the transfer): membership depends on entry in the register of members, so a refusal to register under a power in the articles leaves the transferee holding an equitable interest only. Option A is wrong because executing and delivering the form transfers the beneficial interest but does not make the transferee a member.

question: A company allots shares to a supplier in exchange for machinery rather than for cash. An existing shareholder complains that the shares were not offered to him first, and claims that his statutory pre emption rights have been breached. Is that complaint well founded?
options: Yes, because pre emption rights apply to any allotment of equity securities made.
Yes, unless the articles expressly exclude pre emption on allotments for a non cash asset.
No, because the statutory rights apply only where the allottee is not already a member.
No, because the statutory rights apply to equity securities allotted for cash.
explanation: The correct answer is D (No, because the statutory rights apply to equity securities allotted for cash): the statutory pre emption regime is confined to allotments for cash consideration, so an allotment for machinery falls outside it. Option A overstates the reach of the right by ignoring the cash requirement, which is the limit that makes a non cash allotment a common way of introducing a new shareholder.

question: A private company calls a general meeting to consider an ordinary resolution. The company secretary asks how much notice must be given to the members, on the footing that nobody has been asked to agree to short notice. Which period does the Companies Act 2006 require?
options: Fourteen clear days' notice to every member entitled to receive notice of it.
Twenty one clear days' notice, being the period required for a company's annual meeting.
Seven clear days' notice, because the resolution to be proposed is an ordinary one.
Twenty eight clear days' notice, matching the special notice period for removing a director.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Fourteen clear days' notice to every member entitled to receive notice of it): the default period for a general meeting of a private company is fourteen clear days, and it does not vary with the type of resolution proposed. Option C is wrong because the notice period is not shortened simply because the resolution is an ordinary one rather than a special one.

question: Three friends set up a company, each taking a third of the shares on the understanding that each would be a director and would share in the management. Two of them later remove the third from the board by ordinary resolution and stop paying dividends. What is her best remedy?
options: A derivative claim, because the removal was a wrong done to the company itself.
A claim on the articles, because removal by ordinary resolution is itself unlawful.
A petition alleging unfair prejudice, seeking an order that they buy her shares.
A claim for wrongful dismissal, which would restore her to the board of directors.
explanation: The correct answer is C (A petition alleging unfair prejudice, seeking an order that they buy her shares): where members associate on the understanding that each will participate in management, exclusion from the board combined with the withholding of dividends is the classic unfair prejudice case, and a buy out order is the usual result. Option A fails because the wrong complained of is done to her as a member, not to the company.

question: A board proposes an interim dividend in October. The last annual accounts showed large distributable profits, but the management accounts for the current year show heavy realised losses which have wiped those profits out. The board says the annual accounts govern the question. What is the correct advice?
options: The annual accounts govern, because they are the accounts filed at Companies House.
Interim accounts are needed, because the dividend must be justified by the present position.
No accounts are needed at all, because an interim dividend is a matter for the board.
The dividend is lawful, because realised losses are left out of account until the year end.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Interim accounts are needed, because the dividend must be justified by the present position): a distribution must be justified by reference to relevant accounts, and where the last annual accounts no longer show the true position the directors must prepare interim accounts. Option A is wrong because relying on stale figures would let a company distribute profits that its accumulated realised losses have already consumed.

question: A company must this month remove a director, approve a loan to another director, adopt new articles, and place itself into members' voluntary liquidation. The trainee asks which of those four matters require a special resolution rather than an ordinary resolution. What is the answer?
options: Removal of the director and adoption of the new articles only.
Approval of the loan and the members' voluntary liquidation only.
Adoption of the new articles only, the other three requiring ordinary resolutions.
Adoption of the new articles and the members' voluntary liquidation only.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Adoption of the new articles and the members' voluntary liquidation only): altering the articles and resolving on a voluntary winding up both need seventy five per cent, while removing a director and approving a loan to a director need only an ordinary resolution. Option A is wrong because removal under section 168 is an ordinary resolution, although it must be taken at a meeting after special notice.

question: A partner in a firm of estate agents orders sixty laptops from a supplier, intending to resell them privately for his own benefit. The supplier knows nothing of that plan and the order looks like an ordinary office purchase. The firm now refuses to pay. Is the firm bound?
options: No, because the partner acted for his own benefit rather than for the firm.
Yes, because the act was done in the usual way of the firm's business.
No, because a partner binds the firm only with the consent of all partners.
Yes, because each partner guarantees the contracts made by every other partner.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Yes, because the act was done in the usual way of the firm's business): every partner is an agent of the firm, and the firm is bound by an act carried on in the usual way of its business unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that. Option A is wrong because the partner's private motive is invisible to the supplier and does not affect the firm's liability.

question: A partnership agreement forbids any partner to borrow more than ten thousand pounds without the consent of the others. A partner borrows fifty thousand pounds from a lender who has read the agreement and knows of the restriction. The firm refuses to repay the loan. What is the position?
options: The firm is bound, because an internal restriction cannot affect an outside lender.
The firm is bound, because borrowing falls within the usual course of most businesses.
The firm is not bound, because a loan of that size falls outside ordinary business.
The firm is not bound, because the lender knew that the partner lacked authority.
explanation: The correct answer is D (The firm is not bound, because the lender knew that the partner lacked authority): the firm is bound by acts done in the usual way of its business only where the partner either had authority or the outsider did not know of the restriction. Option A states the usual protection for a third party, but it is lost once the lender has actual knowledge of the limit.

question: A partner retires from a firm of printers. Two months later a supplier sues the firm for goods it delivered before her retirement. She says her retirement brought her liability to an end. No release was ever agreed with the supplier. What is her position on that debt?
options: She remains liable, because retirement alone does not release her from existing debts.
She is free of liability, because the continuing partners have taken over the business.
She remains liable only if she failed to notify Companies House of her retirement.
She is free of liability, because the debt is owed by the firm alone.
explanation: The correct answer is A (She remains liable, because retirement alone does not release her from existing debts): a retiring partner stays liable for debts and obligations incurred while she was a partner unless the creditor releases her, usually by a novation agreement between the creditor, the outgoing partner and the continuing partners. Option B is wrong because an arrangement between the partners cannot bind a creditor who is not a party to it.

question: A partner retires from a firm of caterers. He wants to be sure that he cannot be fixed with liability for debts which the firm runs up after he has gone. His solicitor advises him on the notices he should give in order to protect himself. Which advice is correct?
options: Notice in the London Gazette alone will protect him against every category of person.
Actual notice to the firm's existing customers alone is enough to protect him.
Give actual notice to existing customers and publish notice in the London Gazette.
No notice is needed, because liability for later debts falls on the continuing partners.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Give actual notice to existing customers and publish notice in the London Gazette): a retired partner remains liable for later debts to anyone who dealt with the firm before and has not had notice of the retirement, so actual notice is needed for existing customers and a Gazette notice covers everyone else. Option A leaves him exposed to established customers, who are entitled to actual notice.

question: Three partners contribute capital of ninety thousand, sixty thousand and thirty thousand pounds to their new business. They have no written agreement. At the year end the largest contributor claims a share of the profits in proportion to capital. The other two disagree. How are the profits shared?
options: In proportion to the capital contributed, because that reflects each partner's investment.
Equally between the three partners, whatever capital each of them contributed.
Equally, after paying the largest contributor interest on her capital at a commercial rate.
In proportion to the hours which each partner has worked in the business that year.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Equally between the three partners, whatever capital each of them contributed): the Partnership Act 1890 default is that partners share equally in the capital and profits, and contribute equally to losses, regardless of what each put in. Option C adds interest on capital, which is another default the Act denies, and both points show why unequal contributors need a written agreement.

question: One partner in a two partner firm works full time in the business while the other takes no active part in it at all. There is no written partnership agreement. The working partner claims a salary for her work before the profits are divided. Is she entitled to one?
options: No, because the default rules give a partner no salary for acting in the business.
Yes, because a partner working full time is entitled to reasonable remuneration first.
Yes, but only where the other partner takes no active part in the business.
No, unless she first gives written notice of her claim to the other partner.
explanation: The correct answer is A (No, because the default rules give a partner no salary for acting in the business): under the Partnership Act 1890 no partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the partnership business, so the working partner's only reward is her equal profit share. Option B assumes a fairness the Act does not supply, which is precisely why an agreement should provide for a salary.

question: Two partners have carried on a garage business for eleven years with no written agreement and no fixed term. One of them now writes to the other saying that she is bringing the partnership to an end with immediate effect. The other objects. What is the effect of that letter?
options: It has no effect, because a partnership of that length ends only by court order.
It has no effect, because dissolution requires the consent of all of the partners.
It dissolves the partnership only once six months of reasonable notice have expired.
It dissolves the partnership, because a partnership at will ends on notice.
explanation: The correct answer is D (It dissolves the partnership, because a partnership at will ends on notice): where no fixed term has been agreed, any partner may determine the partnership by giving notice to the others, and the length of the relationship makes no difference. Option C invents a notice period the Act does not require, and the risk that a partner can end the business by letter is the strongest argument for a written agreement.

question: Four partners share a consultancy business on the Partnership Act 1890 defaults. Three of them wish to admit a fifth partner who would bring new clients with him. The fourth partner refuses. The three say that a three quarters majority is enough to carry the point. Who is right?
options: The three are right, because admitting a partner is an ordinary management decision.
The three are right, because a three quarters majority mirrors a special resolution.
The fourth is right, because a new partner may not be admitted without unanimous consent.
The fourth is right, but only if she shows the newcomer would harm the firm.
explanation: The correct answer is C (The fourth is right, because a new partner may not be admitted without unanimous consent): the Act provides that no person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all existing partners, because partnership rests on mutual trust and each partner becomes liable for the acts of the others. Option A is wrong because admitting a partner is not an ordinary matter connected with the business.

question: Two members of a limited liability partnership fall out. One of them negligently advises a client, who sues for the loss. The other member says he must personally meet half of any award, because the two of them are in partnership together. Is that correct?
options: Yes, because members of a limited liability partnership are liable jointly and severally.
No, because the limited liability partnership itself owes the liability to the client.
Yes, because each member is the agent of every other member of the entity.
No, because the negligent member alone is liable and the entity has no liability.
explanation: The correct answer is B (No, because the limited liability partnership itself owes the liability to the client): an LLP is a body corporate, so its members are agents of the entity and not of each other, and the entity owes the debts. Option A applies the general partnership rule to a body corporate, which is exactly the difference that makes the LLP attractive to professional firms.

question: Two accountants agree in conversation to practise together as a limited liability partnership. They open a bank account in the chosen name and begin taking on clients. Nothing has been filed with the Registrar. A client now sues them over bad advice. What is the position of the two accountants?
options: They are liable personally, because an LLP exists only once it has been incorporated.
They are protected, because they agreed to trade as a limited liability partnership.
They are protected, because the chosen name put the client on notice of the entity.
They are liable personally, because the members of an LLP have unlimited liability.
explanation: The correct answer is A (They are liable personally, because an LLP exists only once it has been incorporated): unlike a general partnership, an LLP requires incorporation under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000, so until registration the two are simply partners with unlimited liability. Option B is wrong because limited liability comes from incorporation and never from the parties' own agreement.

question: A client compares a limited liability partnership with a private company limited by shares. She asks which features the two share and which they do not. Her adviser explains the position on legal personality, on filing accounts and on the taxation of profits. Which statement is accurate?
options: Both have separate personality, both file accounts, and both pay corporation tax.
Neither has separate personality, but both file accounts and are taxed transparently.
Both have separate personality and file accounts, but LLP members are taxed transparently.
Both are taxed transparently, but only the company has separate legal personality.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Both have separate personality and file accounts, but LLP members are taxed transparently): an LLP and a company are each a body corporate with public filing obligations, and the difference lies in the tax treatment, since LLP members are taxed on their profit shares while a company pays tax on its own profits. Option A gets the tax point wrong, and that point is usually what decides the choice.

question: A supplier is owed thirty thousand pounds by a firm of three partners for goods sold to the firm. Two of the partners have no money at all. The supplier asks whether it can recover the whole sum from the third partner, who is wealthy. What is the position?
options: It may recover only one third of the debt from her, that being her share.
It may recover nothing from her personally, because the debt is owed by the firm.
It may recover the whole sum, but only once the firm's own assets are exhausted.
Partners are liable jointly for firm debts, so she may be sued for the whole.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Partners are liable jointly for firm debts, so she may be sued for the whole): every partner is liable jointly with the others for all debts of the firm incurred while she is a partner, and a creditor may enforce the whole debt against any solvent partner, leaving her to seek contribution. Option A confuses the sharing of losses between partners with liability to an outside creditor.

question: A company has assets worth four million pounds and liabilities of three million pounds, but its cash has run out and it cannot pay a supplier's invoice which fell due last month. A director says the company cannot be insolvent because its assets exceed its liabilities. Is he right?
options: No, a company is insolvent if it cannot pay its debts as they fall due.
Yes, because insolvency depends on whether assets exceed liabilities in the accounts.
Yes, provided that the shortfall in available cash is expected to be temporary.
No, because a single unpaid invoice is conclusive proof that a company is insolvent.
explanation: The correct answer is A (No, a company is insolvent if it cannot pay its debts as they fall due): the cash flow test and the balance sheet test are alternatives, and failing either one makes the company insolvent. Option B treats the balance sheet test as the only test, which would let a company with valuable but unsaleable assets carry on incurring credit it cannot meet.

question: A company can meet each debt as it falls due, but it has given a guarantee which will almost certainly be called, and once that is taken into account its liabilities exceed its assets. The finance director says contingent liabilities are ignored. What is the correct position?
options: He is right, because only present liabilities count towards the balance sheet test.
The balance sheet test takes account of contingent and prospective liabilities too.
He is right, because a guarantee is not a liability until a demand has been made.
The company is solvent, because it can pay each of its debts as they fall due.
explanation: The correct answer is B (The balance sheet test takes account of contingent and prospective liabilities too): the value of a company's assets is compared with its liabilities including those that are contingent and prospective, so a guarantee likely to be called cannot be left out. Option D is wrong because satisfying the cash flow test does not save a company which fails the balance sheet test.

question: An administrator is appointed over a manufacturing company. She concludes that the company itself cannot be rescued as a going concern, but that selling the business as a whole would give the creditors more than an immediate winding up would. What should she now do?
options: Wind the company up at once, the rescue objective having proved impossible.
Realise the assets for the secured creditors, that being the next objective.
Pursue the better result for the creditors as a whole than on a winding up.
Apply to the court for directions, because the first statutory objective has failed.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Pursue the better result for the creditors as a whole than on a winding up): the administrator must work through the statutory objectives in order, and where rescuing the company is not reasonably practicable the second objective applies. Option B jumps to the third objective, which is available only where neither of the first two can be achieved.

question: A lender holds a qualifying floating charge over the whole of a company's business. The company is failing and the lender wants an administrator appointed quickly, without the delay and cost of a court hearing. Can it achieve that, and if so how?
options: No, an administrator may only be appointed by an order of the court.
No, only the company or its directors may appoint an administrator out of court.
Yes, but only with the written consent of the company's unsecured creditors.
Yes, a qualifying floating charge holder may appoint an administrator out of court.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Yes, a qualifying floating charge holder may appoint an administrator out of court): appointment may be made by court order or, out of court, by the company, its directors or the holder of a qualifying floating charge. Option B is wrong because it leaves out the charge holder, whose out of court route is the quickest of the three.

question: A company enters administration. A supplier with an unpaid invoice wants to issue proceedings against it, and a lessor wants to repossess equipment held under a lease. Both are told that they cannot simply go ahead as they had planned. What is the reason they are given?
options: Their claims have been extinguished by the appointment of the administrator.
A moratorium halts enforcement action against the company during the administration.
They must first obtain the consent of the company's directors before proceeding.
Administration converts every unsecured claim into a secured claim over the assets.
explanation: The correct answer is B (A moratorium halts enforcement action against the company during the administration): the statutory moratorium stops proceedings and enforcement, including repossession of goods, without the administrator's consent or the permission of the court, which is what gives the rescue a chance to work. Option A is wrong because the claims survive; only their enforcement is suspended.

question: The members of a solvent company wish to wind it up and distribute the surplus among themselves. The directors are willing to swear to its solvency, and the company can pay all of its debts in full within twelve months. Which procedure applies to that winding up?
options: A members' voluntary liquidation, supported by a statutory declaration of solvency.
A creditors' voluntary liquidation, because every liquidation involves the creditors.
A compulsory liquidation, following a petition presented by the company itself.
An administration, because the company's business must first be offered for sale.
explanation: The correct answer is A (A members' voluntary liquidation, supported by a statutory declaration of solvency): a solvent company is wound up by its members once the directors make the statutory declaration that the debts can be paid in full within the stated period. Option B applies where no such declaration can be made, so the creditors take control of the liquidation instead.

question: Eighteen months before it went into liquidation, and at a time when it could not pay its debts, a company transferred a freehold unit worth four hundred thousand pounds to the managing director's wife for one hundred thousand pounds. The liquidator asks how to characterise it. What is the answer?
options: A preference, because a connected person received company property before the liquidation.
A lawful sale, because the company received real consideration for the property.
Wrongful trading, because the directors carried on trading while the company was insolvent.
A transaction at an undervalue, made within two years of the onset of insolvency.
explanation: The correct answer is D (A transaction at an undervalue, made within two years of the onset of insolvency): the company received consideration significantly less in value than it gave, within the two year period, at a time when it was unable to pay its debts, so the court may restore the position. Option A is wrong because a preference concerns improving the position of an existing creditor, which the director's wife was not.

question: Four months before liquidation, an insolvent company repaid in full an unsecured loan owed to the finance director's brother, while leaving its trade creditors unpaid. The liquidator wants that payment set aside. What must be shown, and what assists the liquidator on these facts?
options: Only that the creditor was paid in full, which settles the matter against a connected person.
That the company was solvent at the time, which the director's brother must disprove.
A desire to prefer, which is presumed where the creditor is a connected person.
That the payment was made within six months, a period that cannot be extended.
explanation: The correct answer is C (A desire to prefer, which is presumed where the creditor is a connected person): a preference requires that the company was influenced by a desire to put the creditor in a better position than on a liquidation, and that desire is presumed for a connected person, who also has a two year relevant period rather than six months. Option D applies the shorter period, which is reserved for unconnected creditors.

question: A director realised eight months ago that there was no reasonable prospect of the company avoiding insolvent liquidation. He carried on ordering stock on credit and took no advice at all. The company is now in liquidation with a much larger deficiency. What claim does the liquidator have?
options: Wrongful trading, so the court may order him to contribute to the company's assets.
Fraudulent trading, because trading on while insolvent is dishonest conduct in itself.
No claim, because a director owes duties to the members rather than the creditors.
A preference claim, because the later suppliers were paid ahead of the earlier ones.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Wrongful trading, so the court may order him to contribute to the company's assets): wrongful trading arises where a director knew or ought to have concluded that insolvent liquidation could not be avoided and did not take every step to minimise the loss to creditors. Option B is wrong because fraudulent trading needs dishonesty, and continuing to trade over optimistically is not by itself dishonest.

question: A liquidator wants to allege fraudulent trading against a director rather than wrongful trading, because the stigma attached to it is greater. The evidence shows that the director was over optimistic and badly informed, but not dishonest. What is the difficulty with the fraudulent trading allegation?
options: Fraudulent trading may be alleged by the Secretary of State and not by a liquidator.
Fraudulent trading requires an intent to defraud creditors, and so requires dishonesty.
Fraudulent trading applies only to a company which has entered compulsory liquidation.
Fraudulent trading carries no financial remedy, so the allegation would achieve nothing.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Fraudulent trading requires an intent to defraud creditors, and so requires dishonesty): the claim depends on the business having been carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for a fraudulent purpose, which sets a far higher bar than wrongful trading. Option D is wrong because the court may order a contribution to the assets on either claim, so the remedy is not the difficulty.

question: A director concluded that insolvent liquidation could not be avoided. He immediately took insolvency advice, stopped taking customer deposits, minuted the board's reasoning and cut costs in order to preserve assets. The company nonetheless failed. How does the court approach his position on a wrongful trading claim?
options: He is liable, because the company went into insolvent liquidation despite the steps taken.
He is liable, because only resigning from the board can protect a director here.
He escapes liability, because he acted honestly throughout the whole of that period.
He escapes liability if he took every step to minimise the loss to creditors.
explanation: The correct answer is D (He escapes liability if he took every step to minimise the loss to creditors): the statutory defence turns on whether the director took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to creditors, judged by the standard of a reasonably diligent person. Option C is wrong because honesty alone is no answer; the question is what steps were actually taken once the position was clear.

question: A solicitor advises the board of a company which is close to insolvency but still trading. The directors ask what to do about a pressing creditor threatening proceedings, and about a warehouse which they could sell cheaply to a company owned by one of them. What is the best advice?
options: Pay the pressing creditor first and sell the warehouse in order to raise cash quickly.
Continue trading as normal, since the company has not entered any formal procedure.
Take insolvency advice at once, prefer no creditor and do not sell assets cheaply.
Resign from the board immediately, which brings any personal exposure to an end.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Take insolvency advice at once, prefer no creditor and do not sell assets cheaply): as insolvency approaches the directors must shift their focus to the creditors as a whole, and paying one creditor ahead of others or selling to a connected party at a low price invites preference and undervalue claims. Option D is wrong because resignation does not undo exposure for the period in which the director acted.

question: A director has been found to have carried on the company's business with intent to defraud its creditors. The liquidator asks what consequences may follow beyond an order that he personally contribute to the company's assets in the liquidation. Which answer is correct?
options: He may be fined but cannot be prevented from acting as a director again.
He may be disqualified from acting as a director for up to fifteen years.
He may be disqualified for at most five years, running from the date of liquidation.
He must be made bankrupt before any disqualification order can be considered.
explanation: The correct answer is B (He may be disqualified from acting as a director for up to fifteen years): both wrongful and fraudulent trading may lead to a disqualification order, and fifteen years is the maximum period. Option C understates the maximum, and the length matters because disqualification, not the contribution order, is often the more serious practical consequence for the individual.

question: A solicitor who is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority advises a client on the merits of buying shares in a quoted company, and then arranges the purchase through a broker. She asks about her own position. What does section 19 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 provide?
options: The prohibition applies only to firms holding client money in the course of business.
The prohibition is a civil matter only, so the agreement remains fully enforceable.
No person may carry on a regulated activity unless that person is authorised or exempt.
Solicitors fall outside the regime entirely, because they are regulated by the SRA.
explanation: The correct answer is C (No person may carry on a regulated activity unless that person is authorised or exempt): the general prohibition in section 19 applies to any person carrying on a regulated activity in the United Kingdom, or purporting to do so. Option D is wrong because SRA regulation does not displace the general prohibition; a firm must instead find an exclusion or rely on the exemption for professional firms.

question: A trainee is asked to work out whether a piece of advice her firm gave amounts to a regulated activity. She asks what must be established before the general prohibition in section 19 can bite on the firm's work. Which answer sets out the correct elements?
options: A specified activity, carried on by way of business, relating to a specified investment.
A specified investment, held by the client, and a fee charged for the work.
Advice given in writing, relating to land, and given to a private individual.
An activity carried on for profit, in the United Kingdom, by an incorporated body.
explanation: The correct answer is A (A specified activity, carried on by way of business, relating to a specified investment): all three limbs must be present, and the absence of any one of them takes the work outside the regime before any exclusion is even considered. Option B is wrong because charging a fee is not one of the limbs, although it may be evidence that the activity is carried on by way of business.

question: A firm advises a client on the purchase of a freehold shop, and separately on the purchase of the entire issued share capital of the company which owns a rival shop. The trainee asks which of the two subject matters is a specified investment. What is the answer?
options: Both, because each transaction involves the acquisition of a valuable business asset.
Neither, because commercial property transactions fall outside the regulated regime.
The freehold shop, because land is a specified investment of the traditional kind.
The shares, because land is not a specified investment but shares are.
explanation: The correct answer is D (The shares, because land is not a specified investment but shares are): the list of specified investments includes shares, debentures, government securities, insurance contracts and regulated mortgage contracts, but land itself is not on it. Option C reverses the position, and getting the point the right way round is what tells a fee earner which of two similar looking deals raises a financial services issue.

question: A client is selling her business. The buyer has offered either to buy the trade and assets, or instead to buy her shares in the company. She asks why her solicitor keeps raising financial services on one route but says nothing about it on the other. What is the explanation?
options: An asset sale involves a specified investment, because goodwill is a form of security.
Shares are a specified investment, while the goodwill and assets of a business are not.
Both routes involve specified investments, but only the share sale is by way of business.
Neither route involves a specified investment, so the point is one of caution only.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Shares are a specified investment, while the goodwill and assets of a business are not): that difference is why an asset sale usually raises no financial services issue at all, while a share sale must be worked through the exclusions and, if necessary, the professional firms exemption. Option A is wrong because goodwill is simply a business asset and appears nowhere in the list of specified investments.

question: A solicitor tells a client that shares in a particular company look a poor buy at the price offered and that she should not proceed with the purchase. He gives no other advice and makes no arrangements. The trainee asks whether that is a specified activity. What is the analysis?
options: No, because advising a client not to buy cannot amount to advising on the merits.
No, because advice is a specified activity only where the solicitor also arranges the deal.
Yes, advising on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment is specified.
Yes, but only because the advice was given to a client for a fee.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Yes, advising on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment is specified): advice on the merits covers advice to sell or not to buy just as much as advice to buy, provided it relates to a particular investment rather than to investments in general. Option A draws a distinction the definition does not make, and generic advice about types of investment would be a better answer to the general prohibition.

question: A firm introduces a client to a stockbroker and passes on the client's instructions so that a share purchase can be completed. The firm gives no advice on the merits of the investment at all. The trainee asks whether the firm has carried on a specified activity. What is the position?
options: Arranging deals in investments is itself a specified activity, whatever advice was given.
No specified activity arises, because only advice on the merits is a specified activity.
No specified activity arises, because the broker rather than the firm made the arrangements.
A specified activity arises only where the firm receives a commission from the broker.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Arranging deals in investments is itself a specified activity, whatever advice was given): the specified activities include dealing as agent, arranging deals, managing investments and advising on the merits, so a firm can be caught without ever expressing a view on the investment. Option B is wrong because it treats advising as the only specified activity, which would leave introductions and arrangements unregulated.

question: A firm arranges a share purchase for a client entirely through an authorised stockbroker, who deals with the client directly on the merits and on the price. The firm asks whether any exclusion is available to it on those facts. Which answer is correct?
options: No exclusion applies, because the firm still made arrangements for the transaction.
An exclusion applies only where the client is an experienced professional investor.
No exclusion applies, but the firm may rely on its authorisation from the SRA.
An exclusion covers arrangements made with or through an authorised person.
explanation: The correct answer is D (An exclusion covers arrangements made with or through an authorised person): where the transaction is entered into through an authorised person who deals with the client directly, the arranging activity is taken outside the regime. Option C is wrong because SRA regulation is not authorisation under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000.

question: A client is buying the whole of the issued share capital of a trading company and will run the business himself once the acquisition has completed. His solicitor advises on the share purchase agreement and on the price. Which exclusion is most likely to apply to that work?
options: The trustee exclusion, because the buyer will hold the shares for the company's benefit.
The takeover exclusion, since the object is day to day control of the company.
The professional firms exemption, because the work is incidental to legal services.
No exclusion applies, because shares are a specified investment in every case.
explanation: The correct answer is B (The takeover exclusion, since the object is day to day control of the company): the exclusion covers an acquisition of shares carrying a specified proportion of the voting power where the object is to obtain day to day control, which is why buying an entire company often falls outside the regime. Option C is not an exclusion at all but the separate Part 20 exemption, which is only reached once every exclusion has failed.

question: A solicitor acting as an executor of an estate sells a holding of quoted shares in order to raise money to pay a legacy. She does so in the ordinary course of administering the estate. She asks whether she needs authorisation for that sale. What is the position?
options: An exclusion covers activities carried on in the course of administering an estate.
Authorisation is needed, because dealing in quoted shares is a regulated activity.
Authorisation is needed unless all of the beneficiaries consent to the sale in writing.
No exclusion applies, but a personal representative is exempt from the general prohibition.
explanation: The correct answer is A (An exclusion covers activities carried on in the course of administering an estate): activities carried out by a personal representative or trustee in the administration of an estate or trust are excluded, so the executor may realise investments to pay legacies. Option B ignores the exclusion and would make routine estate administration impossible without authorisation.

question: A firm cannot bring its work within any exclusion and is considering relying on the exemption for members of a designated professional body. The compliance officer asks what conditions must be satisfied before the firm can rely on it. Which answer states them correctly?
options: The work must be charged at cost and be carried out by a qualified solicitor.
The client must be a corporate client and must give informed consent in writing.
The activity must be incidental to professional services, with commission accounted for.
The firm must notify the Financial Conduct Authority of each individual transaction.
explanation: The correct answer is C (The activity must be incidental to professional services, with commission accounted for): the Part 20 exemption requires the regulated activity to be incidental to the professional services provided, the firm to account to the client for any commission, the activity not to be a prohibited one, and compliance with the SRA Financial Services Scope Rules. Option A invents a costs condition which forms no part of the regime.

question: A firm relying on the professional firms exemption is asked to manage a client's investment portfolio on a discretionary basis, deciding for the client what to buy and what to sell. The compliance officer is uneasy about accepting the instruction. What should the firm do?
options: Accept the work, because managing investments is incidental to the firm's legal services.
Decline and refer the client to an authorised person, this falling outside the exemption.
Accept the work, provided the firm accounts to the client for any commission received.
Accept the work and notify the SRA once the first transactions have been carried out.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Decline and refer the client to an authorised person, this falling outside the exemption): discretionary portfolio management is mainstream investment business rather than an activity incidental to legal services, and the exemption cannot be used for a prohibited activity. Option C is wrong because accounting for commission is only one of several conditions and cannot cure work the exemption does not reach.

question: A firm carries on a regulated activity without authorisation and without any exclusion or exemption applying to it. The client later regrets the transaction and asks about the consequences of the breach, both for the firm and for the agreement itself. Which answer is correct?
options: The breach is a disciplinary matter for the SRA and carries no other consequence.
The agreement stands, but the firm must refund the fees charged for the work.
The breach makes the agreement void from the outset and exposes the client to prosecution.
It is a criminal offence, and the agreement may be unenforceable against the client.
explanation: The correct answer is D (It is a criminal offence, and the agreement may be unenforceable against the client): breaching the general prohibition is an offence, and an agreement made in the course of the unauthorised activity is generally unenforceable against the other party, who may also recover money paid. Option C is wrong because it is the firm in breach, not the client, who faces prosecution.

question: A trainee is asked to set out the order in which the financial services questions should be worked through before her firm advises a client on a contract of insurance. She drafts a short checklist for the file. Which sequence is correct?
options: Specified investment, specified activity, by way of business, exclusion, then the exemption.
Exemption first, then exclusion, then whether the client is an individual or a company.
Whether a fee is charged, then whether the firm is authorised, then the client's status.
Whether the SRA has been notified, then whether the transaction exceeds any threshold.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Specified investment, specified activity, by way of business, exclusion, then the exemption): the analysis asks first whether the activity is caught at all, then whether an exclusion takes it out, and only then whether the professional firms exemption can be relied upon, failing which the client must be referred to an authorised person. Option B reverses the last two steps, and the exemption is the fallback rather than the starting point.

question: A firm is instructed by a company on a share sale. Its shares are held as to sixty per cent by a holding company, thirty per cent by an individual and ten per cent by an employee trust. The trainee asks who must be identified as a beneficial owner. What is the test?
options: Every registered shareholder must be identified, whatever the size of the holding.
Only the individual, because a corporate shareholder cannot be a beneficial owner.
Individuals who ultimately own or control more than twenty five per cent, or otherwise control.
Only the directors, because they control the company's affairs from day to day.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Individuals who ultimately own or control more than twenty five per cent, or otherwise control): the firm must look through corporate shareholders to the individuals who ultimately own or control the client, or who otherwise exercise control over it, and check the register of people with significant control. Option B is wrong because a corporate holding is not the end of the enquiry but the reason to keep going up the chain.

question: A new corporate client is owned through two offshore companies, and the client is reluctant to disclose their own ownership. The fee earner has verified the client company's existence and constitution at Companies House and has gone no further. What further step does the regime require?
options: Nothing further, because the client company's existence has already been verified.
Take reasonable measures to identify and verify the individuals behind the structure.
Report the matter to the Financial Conduct Authority before continuing to act.
Obtain a written statement from the offshore companies confirming their own ownership.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Take reasonable measures to identify and verify the individuals behind the structure): customer due diligence requires the beneficial owner to be identified and reasonable measures taken to verify identity, and ownership layered through offshore vehicles is a recognised warning sign rather than an excuse to stop. Option D is wrong because a self serving statement from the very companies in question is not verification from a reliable independent source.

question: A firm is instructed on a company purchase by a client who is a serving government minister in another country, and part of the funding will come from a company in a high risk third country. The fee earner asks what level of due diligence applies. What is required?
options: Standard due diligence, since the client is well known and easily identified.
Simplified due diligence, because a public official's position is a matter of record.
Standard due diligence, together with a note of the funding route on the file.
Enhanced due diligence, the client being a politically exposed person.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Enhanced due diligence, the client being a politically exposed person): enhanced measures are required where the risk is high, including a politically exposed person or their family or close associates, and a party in a high risk third country, so both features here point the same way. Option B is wrong because a politically exposed person attracts more scrutiny, not less.

question: A client is buying a business for two million pounds. He explains that the money is coming from an account in his own name at a London bank. The fee earner then asks him how he came by that wealth in the first place. Why is that second question asked?
options: Source of wealth is a different question from source of funds and must be asked.
It is asked only where the client is a politically exposed person or a close associate.
It replaces the source of funds enquiry once a bank account has been identified.
It is asked so that the firm can advise the client properly on his tax position.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Source of wealth is a different question from source of funds and must be asked): source of funds asks where this particular money comes from and by what route, while source of wealth asks how the client came to have the wealth from which it is drawn, and both must be understood. Option C is wrong because identifying an account answers only the narrower question.

question: A buyer offers eight hundred thousand pounds for a business whose accounts suggest it is worth two hundred thousand pounds, asks at the last minute for the purchaser to become an unfamiliar overseas company, and will not give ownership information. What should the fee earner conclude?
options: Nothing turns on the price, because parties are free to agree whatever they wish.
The change of purchaser is routine, and only the price is a matter of any concern.
These are recognised red flags and the position must be considered before proceeding.
The transaction is acceptable, because the funds will pass through a regulated bank.
explanation: The correct answer is C (These are recognised red flags and the position must be considered before proceeding): a price that does not match the value of the business, a late change to the purchaser or the structure, and reluctance to give ownership information are all recognised warning signs, and together they call for the reporting officer's involvement. Option D is wrong because the use of a regulated bank does not show that the money is clean.

question: A fee earner acting on a company acquisition begins to suspect that the purchase money is the proceeds of crime. She wants to know what she should do next, and whether she should first put her concerns to the client to see what he says. What is the correct course?
options: Raise the concern with the client first, and report only if his answer is unsatisfactory.
Report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer as soon as is practicable.
Report directly to the police, because an internal report would only delay disclosure.
Take no action unless she has actual knowledge rather than a mere suspicion.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer as soon as is practicable): every firm within the regulations appoints an officer to receive internal reports, and a fee earner who knows or suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, must report to that officer. Option A is dangerous, because putting the suspicion to the client risks the separate offence of tipping off.

question: A fee earner in the regulated sector has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering on a corporate matter, but decides to say nothing because she cannot prove anything and does not want to lose a valuable client. What is the consequence of that decision?
options: Failing to disclose in the regulated sector is itself a criminal offence.
There is no consequence, because a suspicion which cannot be proved need not be reported.
The consequence is a regulatory finding by the SRA, but no criminal liability arises.
She commits an offence only if the transaction is later shown to have been criminal.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Failing to disclose in the regulated sector is itself a criminal offence): the duty is triggered by knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds for suspicion, so proof is not needed and silence is an offence in its own right. Option D is wrong because liability turns on what she knew or suspected at the time, not on the outcome of any later investigation.

question: After a disclosure has been made about a corporate client, the client telephones and asks why completion has stalled. The fee earner is tempted to explain that a report has been made, so that the client understands the reason for the delay. What is the correct course?
options: Explain the report, because the client is entitled to know why the matter has stopped.
Explain in general terms that a regulator has been contacted, without naming any offence.
Say nothing but confirm in writing that the firm suspects money laundering has occurred.
Say nothing about the report, since telling the client risks the offence of tipping off.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Say nothing about the report, since telling the client risks the offence of tipping off): once a disclosure has been made it is an offence to tell the client or anyone else of the report or of a contemplated investigation where that is likely to prejudice it. Option B is no safer, because a general indication that a report has gone in can prejudice an investigation just as effectively.

question: A firm has made a disclosure and, on the reporting officer's advice, decides to stop acting for the corporate client. The client writes asking for a full explanation of why the retainer is being brought to an end. What should the firm say in its closing letter?
options: Set out the suspicion in full, because the client is owed a candid explanation.
State plainly that the firm suspects the transaction involves the proceeds of crime.
Cease to act and give no reason, so as not to prejudice any investigation.
Explain that a report has been made but that the firm can say nothing more.
explanation: The correct answer is C (Cease to act and give no reason, so as not to prejudice any investigation): where a firm withdraws after a disclosure it should give no reason, because any explanation risks tipping off. Option D is wrong because telling the client that a report exists is itself the disclosure the tipping off offence is designed to prevent, even if no detail is given.

question: A firm is instructed by a new corporate client on an urgent acquisition. The client says the identity documents will follow next week and asks the firm to press on with the drafting and with exchange in the meantime. What is the correct approach for the firm to take?
options: Press on with the drafting, provided the documents arrive before completion takes place.
Carry out due diligence before establishing the business relationship with the client.
Press on, because due diligence is required only where a transaction looks unusual.
Ask the client's own bank to confirm identity, which removes the need for documents.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Carry out due diligence before establishing the business relationship with the client): customer due diligence must be applied before a business relationship is established or an occasional transaction is carried out, and commercial urgency is no answer. Option A postpones the checks to completion, which leaves the firm acting on a matter it has not yet been able to assess for risk.

question: A fee earner suspects that the funds for a corporate transaction are criminal property and has reported the matter internally. The reporting officer proposes to make an authorised disclosure and to await a response before the transaction goes ahead. Why does the timing of that disclosure matter?
options: It matters only for the firm's regulatory record and not for any criminal liability.
It matters because a disclosure made after completion attracts a higher penalty.
It matters because the client must be told once the disclosure has been made.
An authorised disclosure with consent may give a defence to a principal offence.
explanation: The correct answer is D (An authorised disclosure with consent may give a defence to a principal offence): making the disclosure and obtaining consent before the transaction proceeds protects the firm against liability for the principal money laundering offences, which is why the transaction is held up. Option C is wrong and dangerous, because telling the client would risk the separate offence of tipping off.

question: A firm has acted for a corporate client for six years. In that time the ownership of the client has changed twice and the business has moved into an entirely new sector. The fee earner says that the original identity checks are still on the file. What does the regime require now?
options: Ongoing monitoring, so the due diligence must be kept up to date.
Nothing, because identity was verified when the relationship was first established.
A fresh report to the reporting officer whenever the ownership of a client changes.
Enhanced due diligence, which applies to any client of six years' standing.
explanation: The correct answer is A (Ongoing monitoring, so the due diligence must be kept up to date): customer due diligence includes monitoring the relationship throughout its life, which means keeping documents and information current and reviewing them when the ownership or the nature of the business changes. Option B treats due diligence as a one off exercise at the outset, which is the very error the monitoring obligation addresses.
